title: Recall bank, Q151–319
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall bank, questions 151–319. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A 1-year-old had 3 days of high fever. As the fever settled, a pink maculopapular rash appeared on the trunk. Which virus causes this?
questions.exp: Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum) is caused by HHV-6 (sometimes HHV-7): high fever for 3–5 days in a well infant (febrile seizures are common), then a non-itchy pink rash as the fever falls. Parvovirus B19 gives slapped cheeks then a lacy rash; coxsackie gives hand, foot and mouth disease.

questions.question: A child has recurrent skin abscesses, hepatosplenomegaly and granulomas, with hypercalcaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: CGD (defective NADPH oxidase) leads to recurrent abscesses (skin, liver, lung, lymph nodes) with catalase-positive organisms, and granuloma formation in the gut, bladder and other organs; granulomas can make calcitriol and cause hypercalcaemia. Diagnose with the DHR test.

questions.question: Which ECG finding is normal in a 3-week-old baby?
questions.c: A tall R wave in V1 with right axis deviation
questions.e: Inverted P waves in lead I
questions.exp: Right ventricular dominance is normal in newborns: right axis deviation, tall R waves in V1 and upright T waves in V1 in the first few days, which then invert after day 7 until adolescence. An upright T in V1 after the first week suggests right ventricular hypertrophy. Inverted P in lead I suggests dextrocardia or lead reversal.

questions.question: An infant has chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, generalised lymphadenopathy and oral thrush. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Perinatal HIV commonly presents in infancy with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea, persistent oral candida, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent infections and Pneumocystis pneumonia. Test with HIV DNA/RNA PCR under 18 months.

questions.question: Which is a recognised complication of surfactant treatment?
questions.exp: After surfactant, lung compliance improves quickly; pulmonary haemorrhage (linked to a falling pulmonary resistance and left-to-right PDA shunt) and air leak (if the ventilator is not weaned) can occur, as can transient desaturation or bradycardia during dosing and tube blockage.

questions.question: An infant has chronic diarrhoea, hair loss and a red, crusted rash around the mouth and in the nappy area. Which test should be done?
questions.exp: Zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis enteropathica, inherited SLC39A4 defect or acquired in preterm or malabsorbing infants) causes the triad of periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhoea and alopecia, with poor growth and infections. Low serum zinc and alkaline phosphatase; it responds quickly to oral zinc.

questions.question: Which presentation is typical of niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency (pellagra)?
questions.d: Bleeding gums and poor wound healing
questions.exp: Pellagra: the "3 Ds" (and death) - photosensitive dermatitis (Casal necklace), diarrhoea and dementia. Causes: maize-based diets, isoniazid, Hartnup disease and carcinoid. Scurvy (vitamin C) causes bleeding gums; vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.

questions.question: Before tonsillectomy, a well girl with no bleeding history has an APTT of 120 seconds and a normal PT. Which factor deficiency is most likely?
questions.exp: Factor XII deficiency greatly prolongs the APTT but does NOT cause bleeding, so surgery can go ahead. Other causes of a long APTT without bleeding: lupus anticoagulant and heparin contamination. Factor IX deficiency causes bleeding (and is rare in girls); factor VII prolongs the PT; factor XIII gives normal clotting tests.

questions.question: A child and his family have intense itching worse at night. There are burrows and papules between the fingers and on the wrists. What is the treatment?
questions.d: Permethrin 5% cream for the child and all close contacts, repeated after 1 week
questions.exp: Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei): itchy papules and burrows in finger webs, wrists, axillae, genitals; in infants also the palms, soles and scalp. Treat everyone in the household at the same time with permethrin (neck down, head too in infants), repeat after 7 days, and wash bedding. Oral ivermectin for crusted scabies or resistant cases.

questions.question: A child has fever, refuses to eat or drink, and has red, swollen gums with many mouth ulcers. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary HSV-1 infection in toddlers: fever, painful vesicles and ulcers on the gums, tongue, lips and anterior mouth, with swollen bleeding gums, drooling and dehydration. Herpangina (coxsackie A) causes ulcers on the soft palate and tonsillar pillars only. Give fluids, analgesia, and aciclovir if seen early.

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl who was previously well is doing well at school. Her mother complains that she now spends time alone in her room, joins in family activities less and says it is "not her business". What is the most likely explanation?
questions.exp: Wanting privacy and independence is normal in adolescence. Good school performance, friends and normal mood, sleep and appetite are reassuring. Ask about red flags (HEADSSS): falling grades, loss of interest, self-harm, substance use, low mood, sleep or appetite change.

questions.question: The newborn screen shows high galactose. What is the initial action?
questions.a: Stop breast milk and start a soy (lactose-free) formula
questions.c: Stop all feeds and give IV fluids only for a week
questions.d: Continue breastfeeding and repeat the test in a month
questions.exp: Suspected classic galactosaemia (GALT deficiency) is an emergency: stop all galactose and lactose (breast milk and standard formula) immediately and use a soy-based formula, while confirming with the GALT enzyme assay. Untreated: jaundice, liver failure, cataracts and E. coli sepsis.

questions.question: How does adrenaline help during CPR?
questions.b: It converts VF to sinus rhythm directly
questions.c: It improves coronary (and cerebral) perfusion pressure through alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction
questions.exp: During cardiac arrest, adrenaline's alpha effect raises aortic diastolic pressure and therefore coronary perfusion pressure, improving the chance of return of circulation. Dose: 10 micrograms/kg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes (after the third shock in shockable rhythms, immediately in non-shockable).

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa still wants to lose weight and has amenorrhoea. Which other feature is typical?
questions.exp: Starvation slows metabolism: bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, cold peripheries, lanugo hair, dry skin, constipation, delayed gastric emptying, amenorrhoea and low bone density. Admission criteria include HR under 50 by day (45 at night), BP under 80/50, temperature under 35.5, electrolyte problems and BMI under 70% of median.

questions.question: A child with intermittent heartburn now has difficulty swallowing solid foods, especially meat. What should be done?
questions.e: Upper GI endoscopy with oesophageal biopsies
questions.exp: Dysphagia to solids, food bolus impaction and reflux symptoms not responding to treatment suggest eosinophilic oesophagitis (often with atopy). Diagnosis is by endoscopy with biopsies (15 or more eosinophils per high-power field). Treat with PPI, swallowed topical steroids or elimination diets.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy has pubic and axillary hair (Tanner stage 3) and both testes are 5 mL and symmetrical. What should be done?
questions.exp: Puberty before 9 years in a boy is precocious. Enlarged testes on both sides (4 mL or more) mean gonadotrophins are acting, so this is central precocious puberty, which in boys has a high rate of brain pathology (hamartoma, tumour): confirm with LH/GnRH test and do an MRI brain. Small testes with virilisation would suggest an adrenal source (CAH, tumour).

questions.question: A 17-year-old boy, obese, has bilateral gynaecomastia and small testes. He is tall. Which test confirms the likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): tall stature, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, poor virilisation, learning or behaviour difficulties, infertility. Hormones show high LH and FSH with low testosterone (primary hypogonadism); the karyotype confirms. Testosterone treatment from puberty.

questions.question: A 5-year-old drinks a lot and passes a lot of urine. Glucose is normal, serum osmolality 292 mOsm/kg and sodium 140 mmol/L. What should be done?
questions.b: Water deprivation test (with paired serum and urine osmolality)
questions.exp: With normal glucose, polyuria and polydipsia may be diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic) or primary (habitual) polydipsia. A first-morning urine osmolality over 800 excludes DI. Otherwise, a supervised water deprivation test with desmopressin distinguishes them. A high-normal sodium and osmolality favour DI; low-normal values favour primary polydipsia.

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa has an ECG. What is the typical finding?
questions.c: Sinus bradycardia with a prolonged QT interval
questions.d: Sinus tachycardia with a short PR
questions.exp: Starvation causes sinus bradycardia, low voltage, a prolonged QTc (risk of torsades, worse with low potassium or magnesium) and arrhythmias. Do an ECG at assessment and during refeeding.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy has many café-au-lait patches and a history of seizures. Which other finding is most likely?
questions.exp: NF1 diagnostic criteria (2 or more): 6 or more café-au-lait macules (over 5 mm before puberty), axillary or inguinal freckling, 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform, optic glioma, 2 or more Lisch nodules, a typical bone lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, tibial bowing), or an affected parent. Periungual fibromas, shagreen patches and ash-leaf macules are tuberous sclerosis.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl has pleuritic chest pain, knee pain, a photosensitive rash, Hb 9 g/dL, platelets 100 and WCC 12. Which test is most specific for the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Systemic lupus erythematosus: ANA is positive in almost all (very sensitive but not specific). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific; anti-dsDNA levels and low C3/C4 follow disease activity, especially nephritis. Check urine for proteinuria and blood.

questions.question: A child has hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain, and a bone marrow biopsy shows lipid-laden cells. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency) shows Gaucher cells ("crumpled tissue paper" macrophages). Alpha-galactosidase deficiency is Fabry disease, sphingomyelinase is Niemann–Pick, hexosaminidase A is Tay–Sachs, acid alpha-glucosidase is Pompe.

questions.question: An adolescent took 60 aspirin tablets 45 minutes ago and has symptoms. What is the next action?
questions.a: Give a single dose of activated charcoal
questions.exp: Activated charcoal (1 g/kg) is most useful within 1 hour of a potentially toxic ingestion, if the airway is protected. Check salicylate levels (repeat, as absorption is delayed), blood gas, glucose and electrolytes; treat with urine alkalinisation (IV bicarbonate) and haemodialysis if severe. Salicylate poisoning gives a respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis.

questions.question: A previously well toddler has transient erythroblastopenia of childhood. Which finding is typical?
questions.a: Normal MCV with very low reticulocytes, and normal white cells and platelets
questions.exp: TEC: a normocytic anaemia with reticulocytopenia in a well child aged 1–4 years, often after a viral illness, recovering in 1–2 months. Diamond–Blackfan anaemia presents earlier (under 1 year) with macrocytosis, raised HbF and eADA, and thumb or other anomalies.

questions.question: An X-ray shows that a swallowed coin has passed beyond the stomach into the small intestine. The child is well. What should be done?
questions.a: Give laxatives and repeat X-rays daily
questions.b: Monitor for symptoms and passage in the stool; no intervention is needed
questions.exp: Coins beyond the stomach usually pass in days; reassure, watch for symptoms (pain, vomiting, bleeding), and X-ray only if not passed in about 4 weeks or if symptoms develop. Coins stuck in the oesophagus need removal within 24 hours. Button batteries in the oesophagus need emergency removal; magnets (more than one) need urgent review.

questions.question: How does hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) help children with sickle cell disease?
questions.c: It is an antibiotic against pneumococcus
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea increases HbF, which inhibits HbS polymerisation, and also lowers white cell counts and adhesion. It reduces painful crises, acute chest syndrome, transfusions and hospital admissions; it is offered to all children with HbSS or HbS-beta0 from 9 months. Monitor blood counts for myelosuppression.

questions.question: After a diarrhoeal illness, a child develops persistent haematuria, proteinuria and rising creatinine. Renal biopsy shows crescents (proliferation of the epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule). What is the diagnosis?
questions.d: Acute post-infectious proliferative glomerulonephritis without crescents
questions.exp: Crescents (proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages in Bowman's space) in more than 50% of glomeruli define RPGN, with kidney function falling over days to weeks. Causes: anti-GBM disease, immune complex GN (post-infectious, lupus, IgA/HSP) and ANCA vasculitis. It needs urgent pulse methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide or rituximab, and sometimes plasma exchange.

questions.question: A child had leg pain, then could not walk. There is a sensory level at T10 and a distended bladder. MRI shows demyelination of the thoracic cord. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.exp: Acute transverse myelitis is treated first with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day, max 1 g, for 3–5 days). Plasma exchange is used if there is no response. Catheterise the bladder; check for MOG/aquaporin-4 antibodies (NMOSD) and MS.

questions.question: A ventilated child has a GCS of 3, fixed dilated pupils and no chest movement of his own. Brain death testing is being considered. Which finding can still be present in brain death?
questions.exp: Brain death requires coma, apnoea and absent brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, vestibulo-ocular, gag, cough), after excluding drugs, hypothermia and metabolic causes. Spinal reflexes (withdrawal, tendon reflexes, the Lazarus sign) can persist and do not exclude brain death.

questions.question: A child with a urinary infection (leucocyte esterase positive, white and red cells in the urine) also has protein ++. How should the proteinuria be evaluated?
questions.d: Treat the infection, then repeat a first-morning urine protein:creatinine ratio
questions.exp: Fever, exercise and urinary infection can all cause transient proteinuria. Recheck an early-morning urine sample once the child is well; persistent proteinuria needs a UPCR, BP, renal function and further work-up.

questions.question: A neonate has disseminated herpes simplex infection with liver involvement. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Neonatal HSV: IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours, for 14 days for skin–eye–mouth disease and 21 days for CNS or disseminated disease (repeat CSF PCR before stopping in CNS disease), followed by 6 months of oral suppressive aciclovir. Disseminated disease (liver failure, DIC, pneumonitis) has a high mortality.

questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy has excessive drooling that is harming his dental hygiene and skin. What can be given?
questions.exp: Anticholinergic drugs reduce saliva: hyoscine hydrobromide patches, oral glycopyrronium or trihexyphenidyl. Side effects include constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision and behaviour change. Speech therapy, botulinum toxin to salivary glands and surgery are other options.

questions.question: A child has cough and fever. A lymph node biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Non-caseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis (hilar lymphadenopathy, lung disease, eye, skin and joint involvement, raised ACE and calcium); in young children it can present with the triad of rash, arthritis and uveitis. TB gives caseating granulomas.

questions.question: A child with epilepsy on phenytoin develops fever, a widespread rash, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and hepatitis 3 weeks after starting it. What is the diagnosis?
questions.c: DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)
questions.exp: DRESS starts 2–8 weeks after aromatic antiepileptics (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, lamotrigine), sulfonamides or allopurinol: fever, rash, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes and organ involvement (liver, kidney, lung). Stop the drug, avoid other aromatic antiepileptics, and give steroids if severe.

questions.question: A 10-month-old exclusively breastfed baby has a wrist X-ray with cupping and fraying (flaring) of the metaphyses. What are the expected blood results?
questions.b: Normal calcium, normal phosphate and normal ALP
questions.e: Low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase and high PTH
questions.exp: Nutritional (vitamin D deficiency) rickets: low 25-OH vitamin D, secondary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH), low phosphate, low or normal calcium and a high ALP. Breastfed babies need 400 IU of vitamin D daily. Treat with vitamin D (stoss or daily) and calcium.

questions.question: A 7-year-old attending follow-up has bruises of different ages on the back. The rest of the examination is normal. What should be done?
questions.a: Document carefully (with photographs) and refer to the child protection team
questions.d: Check only a full blood count
questions.e: Ask the child to explain in front of the parents and close the case
questions.exp: Bruises on the back and other protected areas (ears, neck, buttocks, trunk), of different ages and without explanation, suggest physical abuse. Record findings accurately with body maps and photographs, exclude bleeding disorders, and refer to child protection the same day.

questions.question: What is a benefit of delayed cord clamping in preterm babies?
questions.a: Less intraventricular haemorrhage and fewer transfusions
questions.exp: Delaying cord clamping for at least 60 seconds (when the baby does not need immediate resuscitation) improves blood volume and blood pressure, reduces transfusion needs, IVH and mortality in preterm babies, and improves iron stores in term babies, with a slight rise in phototherapy need.

questions.question: What is the treatment of apnoea of prematurity?
questions.a: Theophylline as first-line with no monitoring
questions.exp: Apnoea of prematurity (pauses over 20 seconds, or shorter with bradycardia or desaturation, in babies under 34 weeks) is treated with caffeine citrate, which also reduces BPD and improves neurodevelopment. Exclude sepsis, hypoglycaemia, anaemia and seizures. CPAP helps obstructive and mixed apnoeas.

questions.question: A child had a difficult intubation with airway trauma. What can be given to reduce post-extubation stridor?
questions.e: Dexamethasone before extubation (and for several doses after)
questions.exp: Corticosteroids (dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg, started 6–12 hours before planned extubation and continued every 6 hours for several doses) reduce laryngeal oedema and post-extubation stridor in high-risk children. Nebulised adrenaline treats stridor after extubation.

questions.question: A newborn has symptomatic hypoglycaemia. What is the initial IV treatment?
questions.d: 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose bolus, followed by a dextrose infusion
questions.exp: Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia: IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg (200 mg/kg), then an infusion of 4–6 mg/kg/min (60–90 mL/kg/day of 10%), adjusted to glucose checks. Concentrated dextrose causes rebound hypoglycaemia and vein damage. Persistent high requirements (over 8 mg/kg/min) suggest hyperinsulinism.

questions.question: A teenager has exudative tonsillitis, tender lymph nodes and splenomegaly (infectious mononucleosis). Which blood finding is common?
questions.exp: EBV infectious mononucleosis: lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, mild thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases are common. Rare complications: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (cold), severe thrombocytopenia, splenic rupture, airway obstruction and HLH.

questions.question: A baby on long-term parenteral nutrition develops cardiomyopathy. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.exp: Selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and muscle weakness; it occurs with long-term PN without trace elements. Zinc deficiency causes dermatitis and diarrhoea; copper deficiency causes anaemia and neutropenia; thiamine deficiency also causes heart failure (wet beriberi).

questions.question: An unvaccinated refugee child has fever, a sore throat, a grey adherent membrane on the tonsils that bleeds when scraped, and a "bull neck". What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxin): grey pseudomembrane, bull neck from lymphadenopathy and oedema, risk of airway obstruction, myocarditis and neuropathy. Give diphtheria antitoxin urgently plus penicillin or erythromycin, isolate, and give prophylaxis and vaccine to contacts.

questions.question: A child had a Kasai operation for biliary atresia and has ongoing cholestasis. He develops an unsteady gait and reduced reflexes. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.exp: Cholestasis impairs bile-dependent absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Vitamin E deficiency causes spinocerebellar degeneration (ataxia, areflexia, loss of proprioception), peripheral neuropathy and ophthalmoplegia. Cholestatic children need supplements of all four (water-miscible forms).

questions.question: A study records how long 500 mothers breastfed (in months). Which graph best shows the distribution of this continuous variable?
questions.exp: A histogram shows the frequency distribution of a continuous variable (such as duration) in adjoining bars, revealing skew. Bar and pie charts are for categorical data; scatter plots show the relationship between two continuous variables.

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis has a worsening cough with wheeze and Pseudomonas in the sputum, but does not respond to IV ceftazidime and meropenem. What should be checked?
questions.d: Change to a third anti-pseudomonal antibiotic without tests
questions.e: Total IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis)
questions.exp: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis complicates CF and asthma: wheeze and worsening lung function not responding to antibiotics, new infiltrates, very high total IgE (over 500), positive Aspergillus IgE/IgG and eosinophilia. Treat with oral steroids and itraconazole.

questions.question: By what age does a healthy infant usually double his birth weight?
questions.exp: A term infant regains birth weight by 10–14 days, doubles it by about 4–5 months and triples it by 1 year. Length increases by 50% by 1 year and doubles by 4 years.

questions.question: A 12-month-old sits steadily and pulls to stand, walking around holding on to furniture. What is your assessment?
questions.b: Normal gross motor development for his age
questions.exp: Cruising around furniture at 9–12 months is normal; independent walking has a median age of about 12 months, and the limit age to refer is 18 months. Check for red flags: asymmetry, abnormal tone, loss of skills.

questions.question: An adolescent has moderate to severe depression. What is the first-line management?
questions.b: Refer for psychological therapy (such as CBT), considering fluoxetine alongside it
questions.exp: NICE: moderate to severe depression in young people is treated with a specific psychological therapy (CBT, interpersonal or family therapy) for at least 4–6 sessions; fluoxetine is added (or offered with therapy) if there is no response or if severe. Monitor for suicidal thoughts when starting an SSRI. Tricyclics are dangerous in overdose.

questions.question: A child with ADHD and depression on treatment presents with a dry mouth, urinary retention, a temperature of 40°C and tachycardia. Which drug is responsible?
questions.exp: Tricyclic antidepressants have strong anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, retention, hyperthermia, flushing, mydriasis, tachycardia, delirium) and sodium-channel blockade (wide QRS, seizures, arrhythmia). Check the ECG and give sodium bicarbonate for a wide QRS.

questions.question: A boy has coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, joint stiffness and learning problems, but his corneas are clear. Which mucopolysaccharidosis is most likely?
questions.c: Morquio syndrome (MPS IV) with cloudy corneas
questions.exp: Hunter syndrome (iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency) is X-linked, so it affects boys, and the corneas stay clear; skin may show pebbly lesions over the scapulae. Hurler syndrome (autosomal recessive) has corneal clouding. Enzyme replacement is available for MPS I, II, IV and VI.

questions.question: A 20 kg child has burns covering 13% of the body surface. How much resuscitation fluid is needed in the first 24 hours (Parkland), in addition to maintenance?
questions.exp: Parkland: 4 x 20 kg x 13% = 1040 mL of Hartmann's over 24 hours from the time of injury, half (520 mL) in the first 8 hours. Children with burns of 10% or more need IV resuscitation fluid plus maintenance fluid with glucose; adjust to urine output.

questions.question: How does long-term excess cortisol affect a child's growth?
questions.a: It has no effect on growth
questions.b: It causes tall stature with weight loss
questions.d: It speeds up growth and advances bone age
questions.e: It slows linear growth (delayed bone age) while weight increases
questions.exp: Cushing syndrome (most often from steroid treatment) causes weight gain with growth failure, so the child becomes short and obese, unlike simple obesity, where height is often above average. Bone age is delayed and osteoporosis develops.

questions.question: A 3-month-old had an episode of apnoea for more than 20 seconds with pallor that resolved by itself. Examination is normal. What is the management?
questions.b: Observe with pulse oximetry and do an ECG (cardiac screening) before deciding on discharge
questions.e: Reassure and discharge without any assessment
questions.exp: A brief resolved unexplained event: take a careful history and examination; for a lower-risk BRUE consider a 12-lead ECG and brief observation with pulse oximetry, and educate the family (CPR training). Higher-risk features (under 60 days, prematurity, repeated events, over 1 minute, CPR needed) need admission and investigation.

questions.question: A child has Dravet syndrome. Which antiepileptic drugs can make the seizures worse?
questions.a: Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine, lamotrigine and phenytoin
questions.exp: Dravet syndrome (SCN1A loss of function): prolonged febrile and afebrile seizures from infancy, then myoclonic and other seizures with developmental slowing. Sodium channel blockers worsen it. Use valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine or cannabidiol; avoid overheating.

questions.question: Which is a major risk factor for sudden infant death syndrome?
questions.a: Using a dummy at sleep time
questions.b: Maternal smoking in pregnancy and smoking around the baby
questions.c: Room-sharing with parents in the first 6 months
questions.exp: SIDS risk factors: prone or side sleeping, smoking (in pregnancy and after), bed-sharing (especially with smoking, alcohol or drugs, or on a sofa), overheating, soft bedding, prematurity and male sex. Protective: back to sleep, breastfeeding, room-sharing (not bed-sharing) for 6 months, a dummy and immunisation.

questions.question: A child has fever and sharp chest pain that is worse lying down and better sitting forward. The ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pericarditis: pleuritic chest pain eased by sitting forward, a pericardial rub, and diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression. Causes: viral, bacterial (purulent), post-pericardiotomy, rheumatic, autoimmune, TB. Echo for effusion; NSAIDs for viral; drain if tamponade.

questions.question: Which study design is most suitable for investigating risk factors for a rare disease?
questions.exp: For rare diseases, start with people who already have the disease (cases) and compare their past exposures with controls; results are given as odds ratios. Cohort studies suit rare exposures and give relative risk and incidence, but would need huge numbers for a rare disease.

questions.question: What is the drug of choice for invasive Salmonella infection (such as typhoid) in a child?
questions.exp: Ceftriaxone (or azithromycin for uncomplicated typhoid) is first-line in children because resistance to ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol and amoxicillin is common. Uncomplicated Salmonella gastroenteritis in healthy children is not treated with antibiotics (prolongs carriage), except in infants under 3 months, immunocompromised children and sickle cell disease.

questions.question: Six hours after admission with severe acute pancreatitis, a child's urine output has fallen below 0.5 mL/kg/hour and he is drowsy. What should be done?
questions.d: Give an IV fluid bolus and increase fluids (hypovolaemia from third-space losses)
questions.exp: Severe pancreatitis causes large fluid losses into the abdomen and retroperitoneum; low urine output and altered consciousness mean poor perfusion. Give fluid boluses and generous maintenance, monitor urine output, lactate and electrolytes (including calcium and glucose), and involve intensive care.

questions.question: What can a typical 2-year-old do?
questions.exp: Gross motor milestones: walks at about 12 months, runs at 16–18 months, kicks a ball and walks up and down stairs at 2 years, jumps with both feet at 2–2.5 years, stands on one foot and pedals a tricycle at 3 years, hops at 4 years, skips at 5 years. Copies a circle at 3 years.

questions.question: Parents who speak two languages at home ask about their 12-month-old's development. Which is expected at this age?
questions.a: Says "dada" and "mama" specifically, waves bye-bye and plays pat-a-cake
questions.d: Speaks in two-word sentences in both languages
questions.exp: At 12 months: 1–3 words with meaning, understands simple commands with gestures, waves, claps, pincer grasp, cruises or walks. Bilingual children reach language milestones at the same time when both languages are counted together; parents should keep using their own languages.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy is brought in by police after being found in the street. He is agitated and shouting, and substance use is suspected. What should be done first?
questions.a: Ask the police to take him to custody
questions.b: Lock him in a room until he calms down
questions.d: Check his blood glucose and send a toxicology screen, with a full assessment
questions.exp: Acute agitation can be caused by hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury, infection, intoxication or withdrawal. Assess ABC and glucose immediately, examine for injury, take a toxicology screen, and use de-escalation before sedation. Consider safeguarding and mental health needs.

questions.question: A 3-month-old is pale, feeds poorly and is failing to thrive. Blood tests show low sodium, low potassium and a metabolic alkalosis. He had pneumonia last month. What investigation is needed?
questions.exp: Cystic fibrosis can present in infancy with salt loss through sweat: hyponatraemic, hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (pseudo-Bartter syndrome), especially in hot climates, plus failure to thrive and chest infections. Newborn screening may have been missed. Confirm with a sweat test and CFTR genetics.

questions.question: A 13-year-old with congenital adrenal hyperplasia takes hydrocortisone. If the treatment is too low (under-replacement), what happens to growth?
questions.c: Androgen excess speeds up bone maturation, with early fusion and short adult height
questions.e: He becomes very tall as an adult
questions.exp: In CAH, too little hydrocortisone lets ACTH drive adrenal androgens, causing fast growth, advanced bone age, early epiphyseal fusion, precocious puberty and short final height. Too much hydrocortisone suppresses growth and causes weight gain. Monitor growth velocity, bone age, 17-OHP and androstenedione.

questions.question: Two weeks after a skin infection, a child has breathlessness, periorbital oedema, cola-coloured urine and high blood pressure. What is the first treatment?
questions.c: Furosemide with fluid and salt restriction
questions.exp: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis causes fluid overload from salt and water retention: oedema, hypertension, pulmonary oedema. Treat with fluid and salt restriction and a loop diuretic (furosemide); add a vasodilator (nifedipine, amlodipine, hydralazine) if hypertension persists. C3 is low and recovers in 6–8 weeks.

questions.question: A well 5-year-old has a soft ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border with a fixed split second heart sound and a mid-diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. What is the diagnosis?
questions.d: Moderate to large atrial septal defect
questions.exp: A large ASD causes increased flow across the pulmonary valve (ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge) and across the tricuspid valve (mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal edge), with a widely FIXED split S2. Most secundum ASDs are closed by a device at 3–5 years if large.

questions.question: A newborn has respiratory distress after a vaginal delivery, and the chest X-ray shows bowel loops in the left chest. Bag-mask ventilation did not help. What should be done?
questions.b: Emergency surgery within the first hour
questions.c: Immediate intubation and ventilation with a nasogastric tube to decompress the gut
questions.exp: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: avoid bag-mask ventilation, which inflates the bowel in the chest. Intubate immediately, put in a large gastric tube on suction, use gentle ventilation (avoid high pressures), and treat pulmonary hypertension. Surgery is delayed until the baby is stable.

questions.question: A 3-day-old baby born at home (no newborn screening) has lethargy, vomiting and dystonia. Tests show ketosis and hypoglycaemia with a normal ammonia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: MSUD (branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency) presents in the first week with poor feeding, lethargy, abnormal movements (dystonia, "fencing"), cerebral oedema, ketosis and a sweet maple-syrup smell, often with near-normal ammonia. Raised leucine, isoleucine, valine and alloisoleucine confirm it. MCAD causes HYPOketotic hypoglycaemia.
